en: This *Gauragaṇoddeśadīpikā* is the work of the poet Karṇapūra, the illustrious Paramānandana Sena.
In the land of Śrī Vṛndāvana, [he who was] once dense with the bliss of existence, consciousness, and joy...
The dark-complexioned Lord danced with fair-limbed women of similar luster;
by virtue of their constant and most firm embraces, does He not, becoming fair-limbed, conquer Navadvīpa as He takes hold of it? ||1||

We pay homage to this very Lord, whose heart is tender toward his beloved attendants, who brings about the destruction of the flood of sins in the world, and who possesses Advaita and others as his dear followers—
all of whom share equal love, possess an equal array of virtues, and are endowed with equal compassion.
We also pay homage to these [deities] such as Svarūpā, who are full of grace and sweetness. ||2||
We bow to our Guru, named Śrīnātha, the moon in the lineage of the lords of the earth,
the jewel that adorns this world as its beloved;
for when his unfolding secret of Vṛndāvana, free from all impurity, shall manifest—
Having obtained the taste of this discourse, no person in the world remains undelighted. ||3||
With supreme devotion, I bow to my father, Śrī Śivānanda, the lamp of the Sena lineage and the foremost attendant of the Great Lord. (4)
Those who were the renowned attendants of Śrī Caitanya Mahāprabhu,
and those of Nityānanda and Advaita— of those great souls as well.
And whatever ancient names of the Gopālas there may be,
they have been revealed by the original teachers in their respective texts through their essential forms and other characteristics.
Having observed other [works] by saintly persons residing in Mathurā and Oḍra,
and having heard them from the mouths of those belonging to Gauḍa as well, [I have composed this] according to my own intellect.
Having discerned them, I shall write down those [verses] which have been repeated by some;
I am named Śrī Paramānandadāsa, one who has served the eternal teaching. 5.
Just as in former times Kṛṣṇacandra, though consisting of the five elements, became manifest,
so too has the fair-complexioned Lord become manifest.
Since reality is non-different from [the Self], it is here called the "fivefold reality" (pañcatattva);
otherwise, due to the lack of connection with that, it would be a "fourfold reality. (7)
Whatever is different from that, let it be perceived here as non-different from that;
for by his own will and power, Kṛṣṇa has attained such a state. (8)
Therefore, in the *Tattvanirūpaṇa*, Svarūpacaraṇa stated:
"In this [work], the fivefold nature of reality is demonstrated here through the distinction of limiting adjuncts (*upādhi*). (9)

I bow to Kṛṣṇa, who consists of the five principles (pañcatattva), whose essential nature is the form of the devotee, who is the incarnation for the sake of devotion, who is named Bhakti, and who possesses the power of devotion. 10.
The meaning of this, as explained by them, is here written in brief:
since Gauracandra is of the nature of devotion, he is the son of Nanda.
He who is Śrī Halāyudha in Vraja, whose very nature is devotion and eternal bliss;
he who is the teacher Advaita, an incarnation for the sake of devotees, who is Śrī Sadāśiva.
Śrīnivāsa and others are known as devotees because they are incarnations of devotion;
O foremost of the twice-born, Śrī Gadādharapaṇḍita is the power of devotion itself.
Here, these three— the venerable Viśvambhara, Advaita, and Nityānandāvadhūta—
are to be understood as both his forms and his sources of manifestation.
The one great Lord is to be known as Śrī Caitanya, the ocean of mercy;
there are two illustrious Lords, Nityānanda and Advaita, who possess great magnanimity.
The forms of the Gosvāmīs, those twice-born ones, Gadādhara, these who consist of the five principles, and the scholar Śrīnivāsa—[all these are present]. (12)
As it was stated there by the lotus feet of Gosvāmī Śrī Svarūpa:
"In this context, three forms are to be known, and these three are the sources [of authority] here.
One is to be known as the Great Lord (Mahāprabhu), and two are accepted by the virtuous as Lords (Prabhū). (13)
Those great hosts of attendants who have been proclaimed—
all these groups of eternal bliss are cowherds dressed in the attire of cowherds.
O best of cowherds, through association and contact with these [sages], [you have attained this state]. ||14||
There, in the illustrious Navadvīpa near Viśvambhara, those most exalted Vaiṣṇavas indeed shone forth; they are truly to be known as such. 15.
Those who are renowned on Nīlācala are indeed to be known as the most eminent;

those with whom the Great Lord has association while traveling toward the southern and other directions—each of them should be considered great, and others should be understood according to their own fitness. ||16||
Therefore, Svarūpacaraṇa has stated regarding the definition of "Gauḥ":
"Those who are known as 'mahat' (great) due to contact with the five principles are indeed the great Gopālas; the word 'sthāna' (place) denotes pre-eminence and so forth. (17)
Those of great learning call this place Śrī Vṛndāvana, the connoisseurs of aesthetic flavor;
some people call it Goloka,
while others call it the White Island (Sitadvīpa), and still others declare it to be the Supreme Abode (Paravyoman).
Victorious is this Navadvīpa, whose greatness is most wondrous! 18.

Nṛhari chose to take up residence there; because of his activities, even the entire multitude of great beings came to dwell there. Along with them, Hari’s play, though conforming to their great forms, became truly magnificent.
Wherein even the minds of the worlds were immersed in supreme bliss. ||19||
He who, bestowing a white hue upon Truth, became known as Śrīśukla;
in the Tretā age, being fit for sacrifice, he assumed a red color and was called Unmukha;
and in the Dvāpara age, assuming this dark complexion, he was known as Śyāma.
Thus, this very Gaurāṅga, the moon of the cowherds, shines forth in the Kali age, manifesting his incarnation by name alone.
In the Kali age, four traditional teachers have appeared—
Śrī Brahmā, Rudra, and Sanaka— as they are recorded in the Padma Purāṇa.
Therefore, in the Kali age, there will arise four lineages of teachers:
the venerable Brahman, Rudra, Sanaka, and the Vaiṣṇavas, who purify the earth. (21)
In this regard, the Mādhva tradition is briefly set forth here:
the Lord of the Universe, Brahmā, was the disciple of Paravyomeśvara.
Nārada was his disciple, and Vyāsa became his disciple in turn;
Śuka attained discipleship under Vyāsa for the sake of attaining the obstruction-free knowledge.
His disciples and grand-disciples are many, established upon the earth;
among them is the highly renowned Madhvācārya, who received the initiation of Kṛṣṇa from Vyāsa.
Having divided the Vedas, he composed the *Śatadūṣaṇī* Saṃhitā,
in which the qualified Brahman is elaborated from the standpoint of the unqualified Brahman.
His disciple was the noble-minded teacher Padmanābha;
his disciple was Narahari, and his disciple was the twice-born Mādhava.
Akṣobhya was his disciple; Jayatīrtha was his disciple;
Jñānasindhu was his disciple; and Mahānidhi was his disciple.
Vidyānidhi was his disciple; Rājendra was his servant;
Jayadharmamuni was his disciple, who [resided] in the midst of his assembly.
The illustrious Viṣṇupurī, who composed the *Bhaktiratnāvalī*,
was a Brāhmaṇa named Puruṣottama who became the disciple of Jayadharma.
Vyāsatīrtha was his disciple, who composed the Viṣṇusaṃhitā;
Śrīmat Lakṣmīpati was his disciple, a refuge for the aesthetic flavor of devotion.
His disciple was Mādhavendra, by whom this dharma was propagated;
he is an incarnation of the Kalpa-vṛkṣa tree, residing in the abode of Vraja,
bearing the fruits known as Prīti, Preyas, Vatsalya, and Ujjvala.
His disciple was the illustrious ascetic named Īśvara, a resident of the city [of that name].
He, whose very essence is the fruit of the erotic sentiment, manifested that erotic sentiment. ||23||
The illustrious Advaita, who took refuge in the compassion of Śrī Raṅganātha, indeed experienced both fruits known as servitude and friendship. 24.
Having accepted with great reverence the city known as Īśvarapura, the fair-complexioned Lord flooded the universe, consisting of both the material and the non-material.

Having accepted the most difficult task of assuming the nature and splendor of Rādhikā, even though he is the son of Śrī Nanda and an ocean of nectar both within and without, [he manifests as Kṛṣṇa]. 26.
Even his primordial manifestation, which was previously indistinct within the city [of the body], became agitated in mind upon seeing the dance of the Gandharvas. (27)
Even while remaining in Dvārakā, the Blessed One entered the son of Śrī and Śacī; for he possesses various incarnations through the power of his singular nature at all times. (28)
Just as Śyāma himself formerly entered the dark Lord.
Although they remained elsewhere by the power of their yogic illusion,
nevertheless, characterized by inconceivable attributes, they entered Gaurī.
As it was stated by the venerable Vyāsa within the Prabhāsakhaṇḍa:
"Indeed, those entities which are inconceivable should not be subjected to logical reasoning. (31)
Just as the descendant of Bhṛgu remains even after entering Raghunātha,
so too do others remain in other abodes through the mouth of the venerable Nārada; likewise, they sport together with the Lord, possessing bodies of revealed scripture.
However, whatever the dispositions and inclinations of the groups of devotees were, their movement within Vraja occurred in accordance with those very dispositions. (33)
In the *Gauracandrodaya*, regarding Advaita, the words of Gaura are as follows:
"Some are servants, some are lovers, and one alone is a friend; yet both [of these] are exclusively devoted to Rādhā and Mādhava. A few [are devoted] to the Lord of Śrī Dvārakā."
Some are attached to me in both ways—as friends and so forth—while others have fixed their hearts on me in another incarnation; yet all these are truly attached to Vṛndāvana. ||34||
There was a cowherd named Parjanya, the grandfather of Kṛṣṇa;
having become Upendramiśra, he lived in Śrīhaṭṭa and had seven sons. ||35||
The cowherd woman known as Mahāmanyā, who was most excellent in Vraja,
is that very same person here named Kamalāvatī, the grandmother of Kṛṣṇa.
In former times, those two who were the sons of King Nanda of Vraja and Yaśodā— the very mines of the essence of divine love— who were known by the names Śacīpati and Purandara in Vṛndāvana;
They both became so; there is no doubt in this matter. ||37||
These two entered into the divine Aditi and Kaśyapa,
as well as into Śrī Kauśalyā and Daśaratha, and likewise into Śrī Pṛśni and her husband.
Some say that Devakī and Vasudeva, who were the parents of Rāma and Kṛṣṇa, entered into these two [trees] as well;
otherwise, there would have been no manifestation of the form of Rāma, the illustrious Viśvarūpa. (39)
Rohiṇī and Vasudeva, who were the parents of Rāma and Kṛṣṇa,
became the two excellent brahmins Padmavati and Mukunda;
Śrī Sumitrā and Daśaratha likewise entered into those two.
The full-moon day arrived at Vraja, bringing joy to Govinda;
the venerable Lagovinda was the preceptor who composed the songs, verses, and other works. (41)
Formerly, she who stood in Vraja as the nurse Ambikā, the giver of breast milk, is this very same woman known by the name Malinī, considered the wife of Śrīvāsa. 42.
She who was the sister of Ambikā, known by the name Śrīlakilimbikā, and who partook of the remnants of Kṛṣṇa’s meal—she is considered to be Nārāyaṇī. (43)
Formerly there was the great King Janaka, the sovereign of Mithilā;
now there is also the esteemed Bhīṣmaka, the teacher Vallabha. (44)
Śrī Jānakī, Rukmiṇī, and his daughter named Lakṣmī are manifest in the life of Caitanya; she who is named Lakṣmī is revealed therein just as she is. ||45||
That daughter of the venerable Vallabha-ācārya, moving with her friends to bathe in the celestial pool,
was like the goddess Lakṣmī herself who had descended to earth.
There, he came within the range of the Lord's vision. ||46||
In ancient times, this Śrī Sanātanamiśra was King Satrājit, whose daughter was the beloved of Viṣṇu, the Mother of the World, appearing in the form of the earth. (47)
"In the *Śrīcaitanyavidhūdaya*, this was stated by Kali as a digression:
'Having recognized her as a supreme portion of the Earth and the beloved of Viṣṇu, he married that beautiful woman,' and so forth.
Viśvāmitra also acted as the matchmaker in the marriage ceremony of Śrī Rāma."
The brahmin who was sent by Rukmiṇī toward Śrī Keśava, and that forest-dweller who became his teacher through his actions—[these two were the ones]. (49)
And that Brahmin Kulaka, who was sent by Satrājit to Mādhava for the sake of the truthful marriage, was none other than Śrī Kāśīnātha himself. (50)
By what internal distinction do the Sātvatas make their divisions?
[They are] Satyabhāmā, Prakāśa, and Jagadānandapaṇḍita. (51)
The sage Sāndīpani, who in former times gave the sacrificial thread to Kṛṣṇa in Mathurā, has today become Keśavabhāratī.
He who was formerly the sage Vasiṣṭha, the preceptor of Raghunātha, [became] Gaṅgādāsa and Sudarśana through a particular manifestation. 53.
He who was formerly renowned as Vṛṣabhānu in the district of Vraja is now Puṇḍarīkākṣa, a great-souled treasury of knowledge.
Having attained his own true nature, Caitanya, distressed by separation from Rādhā,
spoke thus himself to his father in the place named Puṇḍarīka.
Being a treasure-house of love, Gaura bestowed upon him renown and happiness;
and because he was a disciple of Mādhavendra, he always showed him great respect. ||56||
The son born from that specific manifestation was considered by the wise to be the illustrious Śrī Mādhava;
his wife, Ratnāvatī, is celebrated by the learned as Kīrtidā. (57)
Due to the non-difference between the part and the whole, the first manifestation (vyūha) is the son of Śacī;
Baladeva, who is the universal form (viśvarūpa), is considered the Saṅkarṣaṇa manifestation.
And Nityānanda Āvadhūta was raised up by Prakāśa, who established the Dharma at every turn during the rise of Gauracandra, just as it is for the Kali age. (59)
His elder brother, the Lord Saṅkarṣaṇa, who is the universal form on earth, having not yet taken a wife,
indeed caused his own majesty to reach the Lord of the City (Śiva).
Having already gone forth as a wandering mendicant, he vanished from sight. ||60||
"May the Great One, who is the eternal bliss and the ascetic (avadhūta), be honored; and may He who is Saṅkarṣaṇa indeed be so honored! ||61||
When this eternal Śrī Viśvarūpa had vanished,
he remained there even after meeting with Nityānanda Āvadhūta.
Then the Blessed One, the Avadhūta whose nature is power,
shone forth like the brilliance of a thousand suns in the midst of the assembly of Vaiṣṇavas.
Saying this to me, Janaka danced.
He who, as Śeṣa, is the portion of himself, serves as the bed and the dwelling-place for Viṣṇu and Kṛṣṇa,
appearing in the form of ornaments such as bracelets upon his own body.
[He who possesses] the secret play [of the Vedas] known by the name Līlā.
The two beloved wives of that high-souled Śrīsūryadāsa, born of the lineage of Revata, were Śrīvāruṇī and Vasudhā, who was of the Jāhnavī line; they were his two daughters.
And of him who had the form of Kakudmin and the splendor of Sāra; ||65||
Some explain Śrī Vasudhādevī even as Kalā;
some declare her to be Anaṅgamañjarī and others the Gaṅgā.
Both views are correct, according to the logic of the ancients and the consensus of the wise.
That very manifestation of Saṅkarṣaṇa known as Payobdhiśāyin became Vīracandra, whose form was non-different from consciousness.
As he entered that [body], Niṣaṭha and Ulmuka abandoned him for the sake of their mission;
the other array was headed by Saṅkarṣaṇa, with Mīnaketana, Rāma, and others.
The Gaṅgā, who had originated from the foot of Viṣṇu, became known by her own name;
she was born as the daughter of Nityānanda, and King Śantanu became Mādhava. (69)
The third manifestation was Pradyumna, who became a dear companion in jest;
he acted as the playful partner for Rādhā and Mādhava in Vraja.
He, whose body is non-dual with Śrī Caitanya, is indeed that very Raghunandana. (70)
The arrayed musician Aniruddha, who was the scholar Vakreśvara, produced joy for the Lord through his dancing, which was born of possession by Kṛṣṇa. ||71||
"O Compassionate One, give me a thousand singers," thus he who spoke these sweet words at the abode of Caitanya. (72)
O Nakula-brahmacāriṇī, the white manifestation of Hari entered that moon-streak as its own self-luminous, non-differentiated nature. 73.
And likewise, the possession (āveśa) should be known as being in the mixed [form] called Pradyumna;
the venerable teacher Khañja is said to be the kalā of Gaura. (74)
Brahmā, the Lord of the universe, is to be known by the name Gopīnāthācārya;
he is the one who is enumerated within the Navavyūha by those learned in the Tantras. (75)
Even that Vyūha who is Sadāśiva, because he is of the nature of an immersion (āveśa) in Vraja, is indeed Advaita Gosvāmī, whose form is non-different from Caitanya. (76)
And he who, having the body of a cowherd, danced in Vraja in the presence of Kṛṣṇa, according to the words of Bhairava in the Śrīśivatantra. (77)
Once, during the great festival of the lamp procession in the month of Kārttika,
Kṛṣṇa, together with Rāma and the cowherd boys, danced with great effort.
Beholding me, my divine guru, desiring the state of a cowherd,
began to dance with his beloved in the playful manner of a whirling wheel.
By the grace of Śrī Kṛṣṇa, Sadāśiva became twofold:
one there was Śiva himself, and the other was in the form of Gopāla. ||80||
He who is Kuvera, the lord of the Guhyakas and the friend of Mahādeva—that Kuvera-paṇḍita is today his father, the preeminent among the learned. (81)
In ancient times, on Mount Kailāsa, which is frequented by the Siddhas and Sādhyas, Kuvera—
the beloved of Śrī Śiva— chanted the supreme mantra dedicated to Śiva.
Then the compassionate Blessed One said, "Choose a boon.
Thereupon Kuvera chose [this] boon: "Become my son. (83)
Thus entreated by him, Sadāśiva, the Lord of Gods who grants boons, [spoke]:
"In another birth, I shall attain the state of being your son. (84)
Having thus obtained this boon, he endured hardship for some time;
then, by the power of the Lord's purpose, he became today the progenitor of Advaita.
The divine Yogamāyā is currently his wife;
she has descended in the form of Sītā, appearing under the name Śrī. (86)
His son was Acyutānanda, the beloved of Kṛṣṇacaitanya;
he was known as Priya, the disciple of the venerable Paṇḍita Gosvāmī. (87)
Some say that he who was formerly Kārttikeya is this person;
others, experts in rasa, say it is the cowherd girl named Acyutā.
However, some maintain that both [theories] are correct because they converge in one place; Kārttikeya Miśra is so called because of his similarity to that [Kṛṣṇa]. (88)
Nandinī is to be known as the wild [variety], and Jayā and Vijayā follow in sequence. ||89||
The wise Śrīvāsa Paṇḍita was formerly the sage Nārada;
he who was the excellent sage named Parvata, the beloved of Nārada, is that illustrious Rāma Paṇḍita, his younger brother. (90)
Murārigupta was Hanuman, Aṅgada was Śrīpurandara, and he who was named Śrīsugrīva was indeed Govindānanda. (91)
Vibhīṣaṇa, who was previously known as Rāmacandrapurī, then said: "This Gaurahari is not the cause of Rāma."
Rādhikā’s mother-in-law, Jaṭilā, did not even enter there because of her duties;
therefore, the Great Lord performed the reduction of his alms-gathering and other such acts. ||92||
The son of the sage Ṛcīka was named Brahmā, a man of great asceticism;
though he was known as Haridāsa, he was born equal to Prahlāda. (93)
And in the *Caitanyacaritāmṛta*, Murārigupta’s disciples describe the son of a sage bringing a vessel of tulasī in the morning. (94)
While his father remained in a state of dejection after cursing that unwashed [boy], he himself became Haridāsa, possessed of supreme devotion. ||95||
Those very eight who formerly possessed the eight supernatural powers, beginning with *aṇiman*, in Vṛndāvana, became eight devotees in Gauḍa, just as they were.
Ananta, Sukhānanda, Govinda, Raghunāthaka,
Kṛṣṇānanda, Keśava, Śrīdāmodara, and Rāghava are to be known as the eight siddhis, beginning with aṇimā, according to the sequence of their limiting adjuncts (puryupādhi). ||97||
The descendants of Jāyanteya remained there as perpetual celibates (ūrdhvaretas), possessing equal vision;
they were formerly devotees of the nine-fold [Veda] and were well-versed in the Śrīmad Bhāgavata Saṃhitā. ||98||
Having become perpetual renunciants today, they replied to Janaka, "They sport just as they do with their Lord, Gaurahari. (99)
Śrī Nṛsiṃhānandatīrtha, Śrī Satyānandabhāratī, and Śrī Nṛsiṃhacidānandajagannātha were indeed the pontiffs (tīrthakaras). 100.
Vāsudeva is named Tīrtha, Śrī Rāma is Puruṣottama, the Avadhūta is named Garuḍa, and the hermitage is named Śrī Gopendra. ||101||
The nine treasures renowned in the world, such as the lotus, the conch, and so forth, are born from within the womb of the one called Nidhiratna; they are dear to the Lord. (102)
Śrī-Śrīnidhi, Śrīgarbha, Kaviratna, Sudhānidhi,
Vidyānidhi, Guṇanidhi, Ratnabāhu, the foremost of the twice-born,
the illustrious Ācāryaratna, and the scholar Śrīratnākara. (103)
Because the blue-robed universal monarch spoke in the assembly concerning the future birth of Gaura, he is therefore called Garga.
Sumukha is considered a cowherd (ballava) by virtue of being the progenitor of Śrī Śacī;
his wife, known as Patalā in Vraja, should be understood as his partner in dharma. 105.
In former times, there was the scholar Śrī Devānanda Paṇḍita, a knower of the meaning of the Purāṇas;
formerly, there was the sage Bhāguri, a scholar in the assembly of Nanda. (106)
Kāśīnātha, Lokanātha, Śrīnātha, and Rāmanāthaka—these four are devotees of knowledge (jñānibhaktas), no doubt, just like Sanaka and the others. ||107||
Because the word *nātha* (Lord) is proclaimed within all four of these terms, the "Four Lords" (*caturnāthāḥ*) are spoken of here just like the "Four [Siddha]sanas. (108)
He who was formerly Vedavyāsa is now Dāsa of Vṛndāvana;
enter him, who is Kusumāpīḍa, for the sake of his mission. (109)
There was a Bhaṭṭa named Vallabha, the son of Śuka, who was himself the son of Dvaipāyana. ||110||
The teacher Śrījagannātha was formerly Gaṅgādāsa, the beloved of the Lord; he who was Durvāsas, the beloved of the cowherd girls, became Nidhuvana. 111.
The wise should know that Ācārya Candraśekhara is the Moon;
the illustrious Uddhavadāsa is also an incarnation through the descent of the Moon. 112.
And for this reason, Lord Hari declared this lord of the night (the moon) to be the illustrious Viśveśvarācārya, who was formerly Divākara. (113)
He who was formerly Viśvakarmā is today Bhāskara-Ṭhakkura;
he who was formerly the brahmin Sudāmā, a mendicant wearing a forest garland, wandered about after obtaining wealth from the presence of the Lord, considering it to be a source of suffering. (114)
Those two who were the gatekeepers in Vaikuṇṭha, Jayanta and Vijaya, have today been born by their own will as Śrī Jagannātha and Mādhava. 115.
Puṇḍarīkākṣa and Kumuda, who were renowned in the realm of Vaikuṇṭha, were born as Govinda and Garuḍa in Gauḍa, dear to the Lord. (116)
"The wise Garuḍa is that very Garuḍa who was heard of in ancient times;
he who formerly bore the name Akrūra is now the lion among the lords of the gopīs.
Thus some proclaim: "Akrūra is the speech of Keśava. (117)
Uddhava, who was formerly supreme bliss, became the city.
The great king Indradyumna, formerly a worshiper of Jagannātha, has now been born as Pratāparudra, who is equal to Indra. 118.
In former times, Bhaṭṭācārya Sārvabhauma was like the Lord of Speech (Bṛhaspati) in heaven.
A certain Arjuna, the son of Pāṇḍu, who was a dear and playful companion, met with Rāmānandarāya and became a favorite of the Lord. 120.
Therefore, the virtuous Rāmānanda daily described the reality of devotion and love for Rādhā and Kṛṣṇa to Gauracandra. 121.
Some say it is *lalita*; that which one person approves of, Gaurī said to Bhavānanda: "You are the lord of Pṛthā. (122)
Even though the Pāṇḍava Arjuna has attained oneness with Gopī Arjunī, the excellent ones call him Rāyarāmānanda. 123.
"Arjuna, the son of Pāṇḍu, also quickly became Arjunīya";
this is clearly manifest in the Uttara-khaṇḍa of the Padma Purāṇa.
Therefore, the noble-minded Rāmānanda Rāya [composed] these three [verses]. (124)
Now, the devotees in Vraja are described briefly, according to my understanding. (125)
Formerly there was one named Śrīdāman, who was now the great Abhirāma;
he was the very man who, with thirty-two people, carried the heavy wooden beam on his shoulders. (126)
Formerly there was one named Sudāman, who today is Sundaraṭhakkura;
and he who was the friend of Vasudāma is the scholar Śrīdhanañjaya. (127)
He who was Subala, the most beloved and excellent, was that Gaurīdāsa Paṇḍita; he who was the very powerful Kamalākara was known by the name Pippalāi. 128.
Subāhu, the cowherd in Vraja who was given the name Uddhāraṇa;
Maheśapaṇḍita; and the illustrious Mahābāhu, his friend in Vraja. (129)
In the past, Śrī Puruṣottama was his friend Dāsa, who was slightly dark-complexioned. ||130||
The son of Sadāśiva was named Nāgara Puruṣottama;
he was born of a lineage of physicians and was known as Dāma, the cowherd in Vraja. (131)
He who was formerly the servant named Arjuna is the Supreme Lord;
he who was the servant Śrī Kṛṣṇa is Time (Kāla); and he who was the friend Lavaṅga in Vraja is that very one. 132.
In Vraja there was a brahmin scholar named Śrīdhara, renowned for his boorishness, who was a source of laughter and known by the name Kusumāsava. (133)
Formerly, in Vraja, there was a certain powerful cowherd boy who was a friend of Balarāma; he who existed then is today the noble Halāyudha. (134)
He who was the protector of the cowherd settlement and the friend of Kṛṣṇacandra by name in Vraja, he alone is Rudrapaṇḍita, the beloved of Gaurāṅga. 135.
The Gandharva who is the cowherd in Vraja, the scholar Kumudānanda. ||136||
Formerly, two servants who were as restless as bees resided in Vṛndāvana;
they became the attendants of the Lord, Śrī Govinda, the Lord of Kāśī. 137.
The two former servants who were stationed in Vṛndāvana, Raktaka and Patraka, are today the two young sons of Haridāsa, serving Gaurāṅga. (138)
The two formerly known as Payoda and Vārida, who were performers of dry rituals, have now become servants celebrated as Rāmayi and Nandayi. (139)
Those two singers who reside in Vraja, Madhukaṇṭha and Madhuvrata—Mukunda and Vāsudeva—have been given as the singers for Gaurāṅga. (140)
The actor Candramukha was formerly that very Kāra, the one whose banner bears the sea-monster. ||141||
He who formerly lived in Vraja by the name Mṛdaṅgin Śrīsudhākara is today Śrī Śaṅkaraghoṣa, an expert in the playing of the damphu drum.
In Vraja there was a dancer named Candrahāsa, who was skilled in the aesthetic sentiments;
he was this very scholar known as Śrī Jagadīśa, who delighted in the art of dance. (143)
He who formerly played the flute and the muralī in Vraja by the name Mālādhara is now known as the scholar Vanamālā, the beloved of Gaurī. 144.
Those two parrots, renowned in Vṛndāvana for their skill and discernment, have today been born as my elder brothers, Caitanya and Rāmadasa. 145.
Now, those various groups of cowherd women who have become dear to the Lord are being revealed according to my understanding and as I have heard it. (146)
She who was formerly Śrī Rādhā, the embodiment of divine love and the sovereign of Vṛndāvana, has become Śrī Gadādhara, the beloved of Gaurī, known by the name Paṇḍita. 147.
Just as he has been determined by the Śrīs in their essential forms to be the very fortune (lakṣmī) of Vraja. ||148||
Formerly in Vṛndāvana there was Lakṣmī, the beloved of Śyāmasundara; today she is Gaurapremalakṣmī, and Śrī Gadādharapaṇḍita is her consort. 149.
Since Lalitā followed Rādhā and was thus full of affection (anurādhikā), she entered that place just as one enters upon the rising of the moon of Gaura. 150.
This too is surely the playful Rādhikā,
and this is indeed Gadādhara, the lord of the brāhmaṇas;
or else, this is Hari himself with his own power.
She became a ford, as did her two companions, Rādhikā and [her other friend]. ||151||
Some have sung that he is the eternal bliss, the celibate student (brahmacārī), and others call him Lalita;
however, the correct view is that [he is so] by virtue of his own self-luminous manifestation. ||152||
Alternatively, the Lord, though fair-complexioned, by His own will assumed the form of Atri;
therefore, Śrī Gadādharapaṇḍita is the very form of Śrī Rādhikā.
She who formerly existed as Candrakānti, the very embodiment of Rādhā’s splendor, is now Gadādhara, belonging to the lineage of servants, in the presence of Gaurāṅga. 154.
Pūrṇānandā, who was the foremost among the beloveds of Baladeva in Vraja, also entered Gadādhara solely on account of her duty. 155.
Formerly, she was the supreme Candrāvalī, the beloved of Kṛṣṇa in Vraja;
now, in the Gauḍa country, she is the poet-king Sadāśiva. (156)
O Śrī Bhadra, today that very woman upon whose breast Kṛṣṇa formerly slept in Vṛndāvana is Gaurāṅga’s beloved, Śaṅkarapaṇḍita. 157.
Those two who were formerly the illustrious Tārakā and Pālyau, residing in the region of Vraja, are now the illustrious Gopāla and Jagannātha, the beloveds of the Lord. 158.
Śaibyā was the fierce Caṇḍī in Vraja, and he was Dāmodara Paṇḍita;
for some purpose, the goddess Sarasvatī entered him. (159)
He who was formerly Viśākhā in Vraja, who taught Rādhā the arts, is today Svarūpa Gosvāmī, manifesting the playful expressions of those various moods. 160.
In the past, in Vraja, the king of poets, the illustrious Vanamālī, the beloved of the Lord, fashioned a wonderful arrangement of hair for Rādhā, who was weary. 161.
She who is Śrī Campakalatā in Vraja, the very form of the life-breath of Śrī Rādhā,
has now become Gosvāmī Rāghava, who resides on Govardhana and by whom the work titled *Bhaktiratnaprakāśa* was composed. (162)
She who was Tuṅgavidyā in Vraja, proficient in all the scriptures, is now the ascetic Prabodhānanda, the Sarasvatī of the songs of Gaurī. 163.
In former times, Indulekhā was a friend of Śrī Rādhā in Vraja;
she is a celibate student of Kṛṣṇa’s servant who has made her residence in Vṛndāvana. (164)
She who was Raṅgadevī in the past is today Bhaṭṭa Gadādhara;
she who was Sudevī in Vraja in the past is Gosvāmī Anantācārya. (165)

Formerly, in Vraja, Śrī Kāśīśvara Gosvāmī was Śaśirekhā; she gave immeasurable quantities of foodstuffs to Kṛṣṇa during the Dhaniṣṭhā festival. She herself is now Rāghava Paṇḍita, the beloved of Gaurāṅga. 166.
Guṇamālā went to Vraja; her sister was Damayantī;
[her sons were] Ratnarekhā, Kṛṣṇadāsa, Kṛṣṇānanda, and Kalāvatī. (167)
In ancient times, Gauraseni was Narayana, the eloquent Vācaspati;
Pītāmbara was Kāverī, and Sukeśin was Makaradhvaja. ||168||
Mādhavī, Mādhavācārya, Indirā, and Jīvapaṇḍita. ||169||
Formerly, in Vraja, there was a very sweet and noble-minded beloved;
he was a master of learning, dear to Gaurī, and beloved by the people of Vraja. (170)
The Bhaṭṭācārya named Balabhadra, the illustrious Madhurekṣaṇā, Śrīnāthamiśra, Citrāṅgī, Kavicandra, and Manoharā. (171)
She who was Nāndīmukhī in Vraja has now become Sāraṅgaṭhakkura;
some consider her to be Prahlāda, but he does not consider himself my father. (172)
Those who were Kalakaṇṭhī and Sukarṇī became Gāndharvī and Nāṭikā in Vraja;
and Rāma, Ānanda, Vasu, and Satyarāja likewise became [their respective consorts] according to their order. (173)
In Vraja there was Kātyāyanī; today there is Śrīkāntasena. ||174||
She who was formerly Vṛndādevī, the presiding deity of Vraja by name, is today Śrīmukundadāsa, the beloved of the Lord residing in Khaṇḍava. 175.
Formerly in Vṛndāvana, the messenger and all the gopīs led the multitude of Kṛṣ�ṇas; now my father has done so. She who was Bindumatī in Vraja is today my Janakī. 176.
Formerly, Madhumatī, the friend of the vital breath, resided in Vṛndāvana;
now, the one named Narahari is the beloved minister of the Lord. (177)
Formerly, in Vraja, there was a friend of Prāṇa named Ratnāvalī;
and there was a teacher named Gopīnātha, renowned for his purity. (178)
Vaṃśī, who was beloved by Kṛṣṇa, became Vaṃśīdāsa Ṭhakkura. 179.
She who was formerly known as Śrī Rūpamañjarī in Vṛndāvana has now become the Gosvāmī named Rūpa and has appeared [in this world]. 180.
She who was formerly named Ratimañjarī, the most beloved of Rūpamañjarī, is now called Lavaṅgamañjarī by the wise under this different name. (181)
Today, that eternal one, who is worshipful to all and whose body is non-different from Gaurī, has entered into him—the eternal jewel among sages—for the sake of his task. (182)
Śivānanda Cakravartin, renowned for his commentary on the *Śrī Mallavaṅgamañjarī*, has established his residence in Vṛndāvana. (183)
She who was Anaṅgamañjarī has now become Gopālabhaṭṭa;
some say she is Bhaṭṭa Gosvāmī, while others say she is Śrī Guṇamañjarī. (184)
Formerly, there was a Bhaṭṭa named Raghunātha who resided in a hut at the Śrī Rādhikā-kuṇḍa, where he once lived with Rāgamañjarī. 185.
Some call this work of Dāsaśrī Raghunātha, titled *Rasamañjarī*, by the name *Śrīmatī Ratimañjarī*; others speak of it under the name *Bhānumatī* due to its different title. (186)
Formerly, Bhūgarbhaṭhakkura had a wife named Premamañjarī;
and formerly, the Gosvāmī named Lokanātha had a wife named Śrīlīlāmañjarī. (187)
Those esteemed women, Kalāvatī, Rasollāsā, and Guṇatuṅgā, residing in Vraja,
sang today the song composed by Śrī Viśākhā,
[addressing Govinda, Mādhava, Ānanda, and Vāsudeva] in their respective order. (188)
In ancient times, there were two maidservants of Rādhā named Rāgalekhā and Kalākeli;
they are to be known as the daughters of Śikhimāha, born from the lineage of Mādhavī. 189.
Mallī, the daughter of the Pulinda, and Kālidāsa have now come into being. ||190||
Formerly, there was a celibate student (brahmacārī) dressed in white garments who was the wife of a sacrificer;
having requested his food, the Lord Śrī Gaurāṅga ate it.
Some say that this celibate student was formerly a sacrificial Brāhmaṇa.
There were two other wives of the sacrificer, Śrījagadīśa and Hiraṇyakā;
on the eleventh day, the Lord ate their food after requesting it from them. 192.
She who was formerly Sairandhrī, the beloved of Kṛṣṇa in Mathurā, is now Nīlācalāvāsa, the beloved of the Lord, together with Kāśīmiśra. 193.
Mālatī, Candralatikā, Mañjumedhā, Varāṅgadā, Ratnāvalī, Kamalā, Guṇacūḍā, and Sukeśinī. ||194||
Karpūramañjarī, Śyāmamañjarī, Śvetamañjarī, Vilāsamañjarī, Kāmalekhā, and Maunamañjarī. ||195||
Gandhonmādā, Rasonmādā, Candrikā, Kalabhāṣiṇī, Gopālī, Hariṇī, Kālī, Kalākṣī, and Nityamañjarī. (196)

The sweet-voiced one, the deer-eyed one, the moonlight, and the one who bears the moon upon her crest—whichever [goddesses] there are, they have been appointed by Rādhā to their respective services. (197)
Having assumed a male form, he played with Gaura and his companions according to their respective natures, each in due order.
The twice-born Śubhānanda, a celibate student named Śrīdhara, composed this Garland of Praises to Kṛṣṇa for Paramānandagupta. (199)
Raghunātha was a certain brāhmaṇa who was an exclusive devotee of Gaurāṅga;
Senaśrī Jagannātha was a noble-minded man whose army was the enemy of Kaṃsa (Kṛṣṇa). ||200||
Śrī Harṣa, accompanied by Subuddhi, and Raghumitra, the best of the twice-born. ||201||
He by whom the six enemies, headed by desire, were conquered and brought under control—he was created as Gaura, whose name was truly meaningful as "Conqueror of Foes. (202)
He by whom was fashioned this manuscript, the river of the love for Kṛṣṇa—the venerable teacher of the Śrīmad Bhāgavata, who is exceedingly dear to Gaurāṅga. (203)
The virtuous, learned, and illustrious Jīva, son of Śrīvallabha, the twice-born Vāṇīnātha, a resident of Campahaṭṭa, was dear to the Lord. (204)
Īśānācāryakamala, the scholar known as Lakṣmīnātha, Gaṅgāmantrin, Jagannātha, and Māmūpādhi, the best of the twice-born. ||205||
Śrīkaṇṭhābharaṇopādhi, Ananta born of the Caṭṭa lineage, the one named Hastigopāla, Raṅgavāsī, and Vallabha. ||206||
Haryācārya, Gaurasaṅgī, Miśra, Śrīnayana, Kavidatta, Rāmadāsa, Cirañjīva, and Sulocana. (207)
Some are great, and some are great preceded by "upa"; since the qualities of both are equal, they have all been enumerated by me. (208)
Khaṇḍavāsau and Cirañjīva, along with Sulocana, were the two most eminent disciples of Nṛhari; they were exclusively devoted to Gaurāṅga and took refuge in him alone. (209)
In accordance with the scriptures, one should not utter the name of the Guru;
therefore, I have not revealed the former name of Śrī Śrīnātha.
He was the first to explain the Bhāgavata-saṃhitā in its proper sequence;
his fame shines as Kṛṣṇadeva in Kumārahaṭṭa.
May all those great ones who have been instrumental in breaking the sequence of my work forgive my offense out of compassion,
having discerned all the virtues of the virtuous.
Brahmā, Śiva, and Śeṣa are not able to describe it. ||212||
They must be guarded with great effort from the Mīmāṃsakas and especially from those deceitful logicians; they should be hidden even from those who know the science of aesthetics (rasa-śāstra).
It should always be given to those who take refuge at the feet of the Guru. ||213||
This *Śrīgauragaṇoddeśadīpikā* has been composed by me;
may it shine within the home of the devotees who are filled with a mass of supreme bliss. (214)
This work was revealed on a day of the month of Caitra in the Śaka year measured by the Vasus (8) and joined with the Manus (14),
for those whose minds are immersed in the nectar of the life-story of Caitanyacandra.
This [remainder] is to be purified, known as the sum of the accumulated white counts. ||215||
